etymology: From Latin garrulitas, from garrio, to prate. Webster 1828 names talkativeness, loquacity, and the practice or habit of talking much: a babbling or tattling.
biblical_def: Garrulity is the habit of talking much, a babbling that does not refrain the lips. In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise (Pro 10:19). A fool's voice is known by multitude of words (Ecc 5:3). Speech is a gift. The sin is the practice of pouring it out without restraint, until sin is not wanting.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines GARRU'LITY as talkativeness; loquacity; the practice or habit of talking much; a babbling or tattling.
webster_full: GARRU'LITY, noun [Latin garrulitas, from garrio, to prate.] Talkativeness; loquacity; the practice or habit of talking much; a babbling or tattling.
scriptures: Proverbs 10:19
In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise.
Ecclesiastes 5:3
For a dream cometh through the multitude of business; and a fool's voice is known by multitude of words.
corruption_summary: Garrulity is now often praised as content, presence, or personal brand, as if a multitude of words were a gift rather than a snare.
corruption_paragraphs: A man can fill a room, a feed, or a pulpit and still be babbling. Webster named the practice of talking much. Proverbs says that in that multitude, sin is not wanting. Volume is not wisdom.
The other dodge calls silence cold. Scripture does not. He that refraineth his lips is wise. A fool's voice is known by multitude of words.
roots_summary: Latin garrulitas is prating. The KJV speaks of a multitude of words, and of refraining the lips. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin garrio — to prate; a habit of talking much.
KJV multitude of words wanteth not sin (Pro 10:19).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun garrulity.
usage: Garrulity is the habit of talking much, not a gift of speech.
In a multitude of words, sin is not wanting.
Refrain the lips. A fool's voice is known by the flood.

etymology: From Latin obstinatio, from obsto, to stand against, to oppose. Webster 1828 names a fixedness of opinion or resolution that will not yield, usually a stubbornness not to be vindicated under the circumstances.
biblical_def: Obstinacy is a fixedness that will not yield to reproof. He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy (Pro 29:1). Rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry (1Sa 15:23). Firmness in the truth is not the sin. The sin is standing against the word of the LORD when it has already spoken.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines OB'STINACY as a fixedness in opinion or resolution that cannot be shaken, or not without great difficulty; usually an unreasonable adherence, stubbornness, pertinacity, and persistency.
webster_full: OB'STINACY, noun [Latin obstinatio, from obsto, to stand against, to oppose; ob and sto.]

1. A fixedness in opinion or resolution that cannot be shaken at all, or not without great difficulty; firm and usually unreasonable adherence to an opinion, purpose or system; a fixedness that will not yield to persuasion, arguments or other means. Obstinacy may not always convey the idea of unreasonable or unjustifiable firmness; as when we say, soldiers fight with obstinacy. But often, and perhaps usually, the word denotes a fixedness of resolution which is not to be vindicated under the circumstances; stubbornness; pertinacity; persistency.
2. Fixedness that will not yield to application, or that yields with difficulty; as the obstinacy of a disease or evil.
scriptures: Proverbs 29:1
He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy.
1 Samuel 15:23
For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. Because thou hast rejected the word of the LORD, he hath also rejected thee from being king.
corruption_summary: Obstinacy is rebranded as authenticity or standing one's ground, even when the ground is against the word of God.
corruption_paragraphs: A hardened neck can be called conviction. Webster already distinguished a firmness that may be justified from a fixedness that will not be vindicated under the circumstances. When the LORD has spoken, refusal to yield is stubbornness, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry.
The opposite error is a man who bends to every voice and calls it humility. Scripture does not praise that either. Yield to reproof. Do not harden the neck.
roots_summary: Latin obsto is to stand against. The KJV speaks of a hardened neck, and of stubbornness as iniquity. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin obstinatio — a standing against; fixedness that will not yield.
KJV hardeneth his neck after often reproof (Pro 29:1).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun obstinacy.
usage: Obstinacy is a fixedness that will not yield to reproof.
A hardened neck is not conviction.
Stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry.

etymology: Webster 1828 defines prevarication as a shuffling or quibbling to evade the truth or the disclosure of truth, a trick for evading what is just or honorable, and a deviation from the plain path of truth and fair dealing.
biblical_def: Prevarication is a shuffle that leaves the plain path of truth. Be not a witness against thy neighbour without cause; and deceive not with thy lips (Pro 24:28). Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another (Eph 4:25). A quibble that evades disclosure is still deceit. Fair dealing does not hide behind a shuffle.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PREVARICA'TION as a shuffling or quibbling to evade the truth or its disclosure; a trick for evading what is just or honorable; a deviation from the plain path of truth and fair dealing.
webster_full: PREVARICA'TION, noun A shuffling or quibbling to evade the truth or the disclosure of truth; the practice of some trick for evading what is just or honorable; a deviation from the plain path of truth and fair dealing.
1. In the civil law, the collusion of an informer with the defendant, for the purpose of making a sham prosecution.
2. In common law, a seeming to undertake a thing falsely or deceitfully, for the purpose of defeating or destroying it.
3. A secret abuse in the exercise of a public office or commission.
scriptures: Proverbs 24:28
Be not a witness against thy neighbour without cause; and deceive not with thy lips.
Ephesians 4:25
Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.
corruption_summary: Prevarication is now often called spin, messaging, or legal precision, as if a shuffle were not a departure from truth.
corruption_paragraphs: A man can answer every question and still evade the disclosure of truth. Webster named that shuffle. Scripture forbids deceiving with the lips, whether the words are technically arranged or not.

The other corruption is a sham undertaking: seeming to take up a duty in order to defeat it. That is prevarication in office, not faithfulness. Speak truth with the neighbour. Do not quibble off the plain path.
roots_summary: Webster names a shuffling to evade the truth. The KJV forbids deceiving with the lips, and commands speaking truth with the neighbour. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: A shuffle or quibble to evade the truth, or the disclosure of truth.
KJV deceive not with thy lips (Pro 24:28).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun prevarication.
usage: Prevarication is a shuffle to evade the truth.
Do not deceive with the lips.
Speak truth with your neighbour. Leave the quibble.

etymology: Webster 1828 defines equivocation as ambiguity of speech: the use of words or expressions susceptible of a double signification. He says hypocrites are often guilty of it, and that it is incompatible with the Christian character and profession.
biblical_def: Equivocation is speech with a double signification, so that the hearer may take what the speaker did not mean to stand by. They speak vanity every one with his neighbour: with flattering lips and with a double heart do they speak (Psa 12:2). But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil (Mat 5:37). A double heart is not careful speech. It is a lie dressed as ambiguity.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines EQUIVOCA'TION as ambiguity of speech; the use of words or expressions susceptible of a double signification. Hypocrites are often guilty of it, and it is incompatible with the Christian character and profession.
webster_full: EQUIVOCA'TION, noun Ambiguity of speech; the use of words or expressions that are susceptible of a double signification. Hypocrites are often guilty of equivocation, and by this means lose the confidence of their fellow men. Equivocation is incompatible with the christian character and profession.
scriptures: Psalm 12:2
They speak vanity every one with his neighbour: with flattering lips and with a double heart do they speak.
Matthew 5:37
But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
corruption_summary: Equivocation is defended as nuance or plausible deniability, so a double heart can pass for careful speech.
corruption_paragraphs: A word that can mean two things is useful to a man who will not stand by either. Webster said hypocrites are often guilty of that ambiguity, and that it is incompatible with the Christian profession. A double heart speaks vanity.
Yea and nay are enough. Whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil. Do not hide a refusal, or a promise, inside a phrase the hearer cannot pin down.
roots_summary: Webster names ambiguity of speech, a double signification. The KJV speaks of a double heart, and of yea and nay. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Ambiguity of speech: words susceptible of a double signification.
KJV with a double heart do they speak (Psa 12:2).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun equivocation.
usage: Equivocation is a double signification, not careful speech.
A double heart speaks vanity.
Let your communication be yea and nay.

etymology: From Latin indolentia, from in and doleo, to be pained. Webster 1828 gives the literal sense as freedom from pain, and the ordinary sense as habitual idleness: an indisposition to labor proceeding from love of ease or aversion to toil.
biblical_def: Indolence is habitual idleness, a love of ease that will not labour. Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise (Pro 6:6). By much slothfulness the building decayeth; and through idleness of the hands the house droppeth through (Ecc 10:18). Rest is lawful. The sin is a settled aversion to toil, until the house falls through idle hands.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines IN'DOLENCE literally as freedom from pain, and ordinarily as habitual idleness; indisposition to labor; laziness; inaction from love of ease or aversion to toil.
webster_full: IN'DOLENCE, noun [Latin indolentia; in and doleo, to be pained.]

2. Habitual idleness; indisposition to labor; laziness; inaction or want of exertion of body or mind, proceeding from love of ease or aversion to toil. Indolence, like laziness, implies a constitutional or habitual love of ease; idleness does not.
scriptures: Proverbs 6:6
Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise:
Ecclesiastes 10:18
By much slothfulness the building decayeth; and through idleness of the hands the house droppeth through.
corruption_summary: Indolence is renamed rest, balance, or self-care, so a love of ease can pass for wisdom.
corruption_paragraphs: A man may need sleep. That is not indolence. Webster named a habitual indisposition to labor, proceeding from love of ease or aversion to toil. The ant is set before the sluggard for a reason.
Through idleness of the hands the house droppeth through. Calling that decay a lifestyle does not repair the beam. Labour is the ordinary calling. Ease is not a creed.
roots_summary: Latin indolentia is, literally, freedom from pain; in use, habitual idleness. The KJV sends the sluggard to the ant, and warns that idle hands let the house drop through. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin in and doleo — literally, not to be pained; in use, love of ease.
KJV idleness of the hands lets the house drop through (Ecc 10:18).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun indolence.
usage: Indolence is habitual love of ease, not lawful rest.
Go to the ant. Consider her ways.
Idle hands let the house drop through.

etymology: From Latin impudens, from in and pudens, from pudeo, to be ashamed. Webster 1828 defines it as shamelessness, want of modesty, effrontery, and assurance accompanied with a disregard of the opinions of others.
biblical_def: Impudence is shamelessness, a face that will not blush. Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush: therefore they shall fall among them that fall (Jer 6:15). So she caught him, and kissed him, and with an impudent face said unto him (Pro 7:13). Boldness for the truth is not the sin. The sin is assurance that has put off shame.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines IM'PUDENCE as shamelessness; want of modesty; effrontery; assurance accompanied with a disregard of the opinions of others.
webster_full: IM'PUDENCE, noun [Latin impudens; in and pudens, from pudeo, to be ashamed.] Shamelessness; want of modesty; effrontery; assurance accompanied with a disregard of the opinions of others.
Those clear truths, that either their own evidence forces us to admit, or common experience makes it impudence to deny.
scriptures: Jeremiah 6:15

Were they ashamed when they had committed abomination? nay, they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush: therefore they shall fall among them that fall: at the time that I visit them they shall be cast down, saith the LORD.
Proverbs 7:13
So she caught him, and kissed him, and with an impudent face said unto him,
corruption_summary: Impudence is marketed as confidence or being unapologetic, so a face that cannot blush is treated as strength.
corruption_paragraphs: Shame is not a defect to be cured in every case. Jeremiah asks whether they were ashamed when they had committed abomination, and the answer is that they could not blush. That inability is the judgment already at work.
Webster named assurance accompanied with a disregard of others. Scripture names an impudent face. Do not baptize shamelessness as confidence. A people who cannot blush are near a fall.
roots_summary: Latin impudens is without shame. The KJV speaks of those who could not blush, and of an impudent face. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin pudeo — to be ashamed; impudence is the want of that shame.
KJV neither could they blush (Jer 6:15).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun impudence.
usage: Impudence is shamelessness, not confidence.
An impudent face has put off blushing.
They that cannot blush shall fall.

etymology: From Latin malevolentia, from malum, evil, and volens, willing. Webster 1828 defines it as ill will, personal hatred, an evil disposition toward another, enmity of heart, and an inclination to injure others. It expresses less than malignity.
biblical_def: Malevolence is ill will, an inclination of the heart to injure. Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him (1Jn 3:15). He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him (Pro 26:24). Hatred need not draw a sword to be murder in the sight of God. The will to injure is already the sin.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MALEV'OLENCE as ill will; personal hatred; evil disposition towards another; enmity of heart; inclination to injure others. It expresses less than malignity.
webster_full: MALEV'OLENCE, noun [Latin malevolentia; malum, evil, and volens, volo, to will.] Ill will, personal hatred; evil disposition towards another; enmity of heart; inclination to injure others. It expresses less than malignity.
scriptures: 1 John 3:15
Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer: and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him.
Proverbs 26:24
He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him;
corruption_summary: Malevolence is softened into dislike, a boundary, or a personality clash, so ill will need not repent.
corruption_paragraphs: A man can nurse an inclination to injure and call it discernment. Webster named ill will and enmity of heart. John says that whoever hates his brother is a murderer. The degree of the wound does not cleanse the will.
Hatred also dissembles. Fair speech can cover deceit laid up within. Do not grade ill will as a lesser temper. Put away the inclination to injure.
roots_summary: Latin malevolentia is a willing of evil. The KJV says he that hateth his brother is a murderer, and that hatred dissembles with the lips. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Latin malum and volo — to will evil toward another.
KJV whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer (1Jn 3:15).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun malevolence.
usage: Malevolence is ill will, an inclination to injure.
Hatred of a brother is murder in God's sight.
Fair lips do not cleanse a heart that lays up deceit.

etymology: Webster 1828 defines venality as mercenariness: the state of being influenced by money, and the prostitution of talents, offices, or services for money or reward, as the venality of a corrupt court.
biblical_def: Venality is the sale of judgment, office, or service for reward. And thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous (Exo 23:8). A wicked man taketh a gift out of the bosom to pervert the ways of judgment (Pro 17:23). A wage for honest labour is not the sin. The sin is a gift that buys the word, the bench, or the altar.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines VENAL'ITY as mercenariness; the state of being influenced by money; prostitution of talents, offices or services for money or reward, as the venality of a corrupt court.
webster_full: VENAL'ITY, noun Mercenariness; the state of being influenced by money; prostitution of talents, offices or services for money or reward; as the venality of a corrupt court.
scriptures: Exodus 23:8
And thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous.
Proverbs 17:23
A wicked man taketh a gift out of the bosom to pervert the ways of judgment.
corruption_summary: Venality is rebranded as access, consulting, or incentive, so a bought judgment can pass for ordinary business.
corruption_paragraphs: A gift in the bosom is still a gift. Webster named the prostitution of offices and services for money. Exodus says the gift blinds the wise and perverts the words of the righteous. The size of the fee does not change the blinding.
Honest pay for honest labour is not venality. The sin is influence purchased, a court or a pulpit that leans on reward and still says the LORD is among us. Take no gift that perverts judgment.
roots_summary: Webster names mercenariness, offices and services sold for reward. The KJV forbids taking a gift that blinds the wise, and names the gift taken to pervert judgment. No Strong's number is invented for the English noun.
roots_lines: Mercenariness: talents, offices, or services sold for money or reward.
KJV thou shalt take no gift (Exo 23:8).
No invented Strong's tag for the English noun venality.
usage: Venality is the sale of office or judgment for reward.
Take no gift. A gift blinds the wise.
A gift out of the bosom perverts judgment.
